course.title: Rocks and Minerals
course.summary: Identify rocks and minerals from observable evidence, explain how rocks form, and make defensible decisions under station timing.
objectives: Distinguish observations from inferences and select diagnostic tests.
Identify minerals using physical properties and an evidence-first workflow.
Classify igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks from texture and formation evidence.
Document an identification so another competitor can follow the reasoning.

units.title: Observe Like a Geologist
units.summary: Build the evidence habits that make every later identification more reliable.
objectives: Separate a rock, mineral, and manufactured material.
Record observations before naming a specimen.

skills.name: Rocks, Minerals, and Evidence
skills.description: Distinguish a mineral from a rock and justify the distinction with observable or structural evidence.

lesson.title: Rocks, Minerals, and Evidence
lesson.summary: Students learn to distinguish minerals from rocks by using evidence such as chemical composition, atomic structure, aggregate composition, texture, and observable physical properties.

content.kicker: Geologists do not just name specimens; they defend their claims with evidence.
content.heading: Goal for Today
content.body: By the end of this lesson, you will classify a specimen description as a rock or a mineral and justify your choice using at least two pieces of observable or structural evidence.

content.heading: Core Difference: Mineral vs. Rock
content.body: Start with the definition, then look for evidence that matches it.

cards.name: Mineral
cards.detail: A mineral is naturally occurring and has a characteristic chemical composition, atoms arranged in an orderly repeating pattern, and specific physical properties.

cards.name: Rock
cards.detail: A rock is a naturally occurring aggregate of minerals and/or mineraloids. Rocks generally do not have a definite chemical composition.

cards.name: Shared Trait
cards.detail: Both rocks and minerals are solid materials, so being solid is not enough evidence by itself.

cards.name: Structure Clue
cards.cue: Mineral structure is ordered; rock structure is not the same claim
cards.detail: Minerals have atoms arranged in a highly ordered three-dimensional pattern. Rocks do not have a crystalline structure as whole rocks, although they may be composed of mineral crystals.

content.heading: Check the Definition
content.question: Which statement best distinguishes a mineral from a rock?
choices: A mineral has a definite chemical composition and ordered atomic structure, while a rock is generally an aggregate or mixture.
A mineral is any solid Earth material, while a rock is any liquid Earth material.
A mineral can contain fossils, while a rock cannot contain fossils.
A mineral is identified only by color, while a rock is identified only by shape.
content.explanation: The strongest distinction is that a mineral has a characteristic chemical composition and ordered atomic arrangement, while a rock is generally an aggregate of minerals and/or mineraloids and does not have a definite chemical composition.

misconception_by_choice.1: This treats solidity as the whole test. Both rocks and minerals are solid materials, so that does not separate them.
misconception_by_choice.2: This reverses the fossil evidence. Minerals are listed as having no fossils, while sedimentary rocks may have fossils.
misconception_by_choice.3: This overuses appearance. Color can be useful, but it is not the only evidence, and mineral color can vary.

content.heading: How to Build an Evidence-Based Classification

steps.label: Step 1: Ask what kind of composition evidence you have.
steps.detail: A definite chemical composition or formula supports a mineral claim. A mixture or aggregate of minerals supports a rock claim.

steps.label: Step 2: Ask what structure evidence you have.
steps.detail: An orderly repeating atomic pattern supports a mineral claim. A rock may contain mineral crystals, but the whole rock is not defined by one crystalline structure.

steps.label: Step 3: Use observable properties carefully.
steps.detail: Mineral properties include color, luster, streak, hardness, cleavage, fracture, and crystal form. Color is visible, but it can be affected by impurities or defects.

steps.label: Step 4: Look for rock evidence.
steps.detail: Rock evidence can include texture, particle size, composition, and classification. A specimen described by grain size and a mix of components is being treated as a rock.

steps.label: Step 5: Record useful evidence clearly.
steps.detail: For a binder page, useful fields include formula or composition, mineral system or structure, rock texture, classification, properties, environment of formation, and uses.

content.heading: Solid Is Not Enough
content.question: A student says, “This specimen is solid, so it must be a mineral.” What is the best response?
choices: Agree, because only minerals are solid materials.
Disagree, because both rocks and minerals are solid, so more evidence is needed.
Agree, because rocks do not occur naturally.
Disagree, because minerals do not have physical properties.
content.explanation: Solidity is shared by rocks and minerals. To distinguish them, you need stronger evidence such as definite chemical composition and ordered atomic structure for minerals, or aggregate composition for rocks.

misconception_by_choice.0: This ignores that both rocks and minerals are solid materials.
misconception_by_choice.2: This misstates the definition of rock. A rock is naturally occurring.
misconception_by_choice.3: This ignores that minerals have specific physical properties used for identification.

content.heading: Evidence You Can Observe or Record
content.body: Different kinds of evidence are useful for different claims. Use the evidence that matches the question: mineral or rock?

cards.name: Mineral Physical Properties
cards.detail: Color, luster, streak, hardness, cleavage, fracture, and crystal form are useful properties for identifying most minerals.

cards.name: Special Mineral Clues
cards.detail: Reaction with acid, magnetism, specific gravity or density, tenacity, taste, odor, feel, and striations can help identify certain minerals.

cards.name: Color Warning
cards.cue: Easy to see, easy to overtrust
cards.detail: Color is readily apparent, but slight impurities or defects can determine the color of many minerals.

cards.name: Rock Texture and Composition
cards.detail: Sedimentary rock charts use texture, particle size, composition, comments, and rock name. Examples include grain size, sandpapery feel, fossils, and calcite composition.

cards.name: Binder Evidence Fields
cards.detail: A useful specimen page may include classification, properties, formula or composition, mineral system or structure, rock texture, environment of formation, and uses.

content.heading: Do Not Overtrust Color
content.question: A mineral sample is purple, and a student wants to identify it by color alone. Which response best matches good evidence use?
choices: Color alone is enough because color is always uniform for every mineral species.
Color should be ignored completely because it is never useful.
Color can be recorded, but other properties such as streak, hardness, cleavage, fracture, or crystal form should also be used.
Color proves the sample is a rock because rocks are the only materials with color.
content.explanation: Color is a visible mineral property, but it can be affected by impurities or defects. Stronger identification uses color along with other physical properties such as streak, hardness, cleavage, fracture, and crystal form.

misconception_by_choice.0: This overstates color. The same mineral species may have many color varieties, and color can be affected by impurities or defects.
misconception_by_choice.1: This goes too far. Color is a useful observed property, but it should be used carefully.
misconception_by_choice.3: This falsely separates color from minerals. Minerals have color, but color alone does not prove rock or mineral.

content.heading: Worked Example: Sandstone Evidence
content.prompt: A specimen description says: fine grains 1/16 to 2 mm, sandpapery feel, quartz with minor accessory minerals, rock name: quartz sandstone. Is the specimen being classified as a rock or a mineral? Justify with evidence.
steps: The description uses texture and particle size: fine grains and sandpapery feel.
The description gives composition as quartz with minor accessory minerals, which points to more than one component.
The chart lists the result as a rock name: quartz sandstone.
A rock is an aggregate of minerals and/or mineraloids and generally does not have one definite chemical composition.
Conclusion: classify it as a rock, and justify using texture, grain size, mixed composition, and the rock name.

content.heading: Transfer to a New Specimen Description
content.question: A specimen description says it has abundant fossils and calcite composition that fizzes with dilute HCl. The chart names it fossiliferous limestone. Which claim is best supported?
choices: It is a mineral because fossils are listed as a mineral property.
It is a rock because the chart classifies fossiliferous limestone as a sedimentary rock and minerals are listed as having no fossils.
It is a mineral because all calcite-containing materials must be minerals.
It cannot be classified because acid reaction is never useful evidence.
content.explanation: The evidence supports a rock claim because fossiliferous limestone is listed under sedimentary rocks, and fossils are associated with sedimentary rocks rather than minerals. The calcite and acid reaction are evidence recorded in the rock chart, but the classification name and fossil evidence point to rock.

misconception_by_choice.0: This reverses the fossil evidence. Minerals are listed as having no fossils.
misconception_by_choice.2: This treats one component as if it decides the whole specimen. Rocks can contain minerals and still be rocks.
misconception_by_choice.3: This ignores that reaction with acid can be helpful evidence for certain minerals and is also used in the sedimentary rock chart comments.

content.heading: Competition Habit: Turn Observations into a Claim

steps.label: Name the claim.
steps.detail: Decide whether the evidence better supports mineral or rock.

steps.label: Choose matching evidence.
steps.detail: For a mineral claim, look for definite chemical composition, ordered atomic structure, and mineral physical properties. For a rock claim, look for aggregate composition, texture, particle size, and rock classification.

steps.label: Avoid weak evidence.
steps.detail: Do not use solidness alone, and do not rely on color alone.

steps.label: Prepare to explain, not just identify.
steps.detail: Rocks and Minerals requires students to identify and classify rocks and minerals and use that knowledge to explain geological processes, interpret Earth history, and understand natural resources.

steps.label: Organize notes for quick use.
steps.detail: Specimen pages should be easy to find and understand, with information such as classification, properties, formula or composition, structure, texture, formation environment, and uses.

content.heading: Choose the Best Binder Evidence
content.question: You are making two binder pages: one for a mineral specimen and one for a rock specimen. Which pair of evidence fields best helps distinguish them?
choices: Mineral: formula and mineral system/structure; Rock: rock classification and rock texture.
Mineral: rock texture; Rock: mineral system/structure.
Mineral: fossils; Rock: definite chemical formula only.
Mineral: color only; Rock: color only.
content.explanation: Formula and mineral system or structure match mineral evidence because minerals have characteristic chemical composition and ordered atomic arrangement. Rock classification and rock texture match rock evidence because rocks are classified using features such as texture, composition, and rock type.

misconception_by_choice.1: This swaps the evidence. Mineral system or structure is a mineral field, while rock texture is a rock field.
misconception_by_choice.2: This reverses key evidence. Minerals are listed as having no fossils, and rocks do not have a definite chemical composition.
misconception_by_choice.3: This relies only on color. Color can be useful, but it is not enough to distinguish rock from mineral.

content.heading: Key Points
points: A mineral has a characteristic chemical composition and an ordered atomic structure.
A rock is a naturally occurring aggregate of minerals and/or mineraloids and generally does not have a definite chemical composition.
Both rocks and minerals are solid, so solidness alone is not a deciding clue.
Mineral evidence includes properties such as streak, hardness, cleavage, fracture, luster, crystal form, and sometimes acid reaction or magnetism.
Rock evidence includes texture, particle size, composition, fossils in sedimentary rocks, and rock classification.
A strong answer makes a claim and supports it with matching evidence.
content.next_step: Practice with three specimen descriptions: label each as rock or mineral, then write two evidence statements for each choice.

skills.name: Observe Before You Identify
skills.description: Separate observation from inference and record a repeatable evidence profile.

lesson.title: Observe Before You Identify
lesson.summary: Students learn to separate direct evidence from identification conclusions by recording physical properties, test results, and station information in an organized evidence profile before naming a rock or mineral.

content.kicker: Geologists do not start with a name; they start with evidence.
content.heading: Measurable Goal
content.body: By the end of this lesson, you will write an evidence profile for an unknown rock or mineral that separates observations and test results from the final identification.

content.title: RocksMinerals27
content.transcript_excerpt: Focus on Video 05:03–05:51; the notes and checks that follow use the retained transcript.

content.heading: Evidence First: What Belongs in the Profile?
content.body: A repeatable evidence profile records what can be observed or tested before deciding on an identification.

cards.name: Physical properties
cards.detail: Mineral identification moves from observing physical properties of an unknown mineral toward an accurate identification.

cards.name: Tools and tests
cards.cue: Hand lens, streak plate, copper penny, glass plate or steel knife, magnet, dilute hydrochloric acid
cards.detail: The listed tools and equipment support determining mineral properties, so the profile should record the property information gathered from allowed tools.

cards.name: Organization
cards.detail: Rocks and Minerals rewards careful, organized information because students may need to perform and interpret hands-on tests.

content.heading: Observation or Conclusion?
content.question: Which notebook entry best separates evidence from an identification conclusion for an unknown mineral?
choices: Specimen is probably Mineral A; no properties recorded.
Hand lens used; luster, hardness, streak, and cleavage fields recorded before naming.
It looks interesting, so it belongs in geology.
Skip the properties and match it to the first familiar name.
content.explanation: The strongest entry records physical-property evidence first. Mineral identification is described as moving from observed physical properties of an unknown to an accurate identification, and successful students need attention to detail and organized information.

misconception_by_choice.0: This jumps to an identification without a repeatable evidence profile.
misconception_by_choice.2: Interest in geology is helpful, but it is not evidence for identifying the specimen.
misconception_by_choice.3: A familiar name is an inference, not a recorded observation or test result.

content.heading: A Station Routine for Evidence Profiles

steps.label: Read the task
steps.detail: A station is usually based around a specimen, sample, data, or something unique to that station.

steps.label: Record the specimen label
steps.detail: Use the station’s labels, such as Specimen A or Mineral A, so every observation stays connected to the correct item.

steps.label: Capture evidence quickly
steps.detail: Stations have limited time, so record the most useful observations and allowed test results in an organized way.

steps.label: Do not plan to return
steps.detail: Once time is up and you leave a station, there is no going back to that station.

steps.label: Infer last
steps.detail: Use the evidence profile to answer identification or property questions after the observations are recorded.

content.heading: Why Record Before You Move?
content.question: During a stations test, why is it especially important to record a repeatable evidence profile before leaving a station?
choices: Because students can always come back later and improve their notes.
Because stations have limited time, and once students leave, they are done with that station.
Because only collecting rocks matters in this event.
Because correct answers are not counted in test events.
content.explanation: A stations format has limited time, and students move on when time is up. Since there is no going back, the evidence profile must be complete enough to support answers before leaving.

misconception_by_choice.0: The station format specifically says there is no going back after leaving.
misconception_by_choice.2: Interest in collecting can fit the event, but competition work is based on questions, specimens, samples, data, and tests.
misconception_by_choice.3: Points are awarded based on the number of correct answers students provide.

content.heading: Common Evidence Fields
content.body: Use property fields that match what competitions and identification guides ask students to observe, test, or interpret.

cards.name: Luster
cards.detail: A mineral identification flowchart begins by checking luster.

cards.name: Hardness
cards.cue: Hardness below or above 5.5; increasing hardness
cards.detail: The flowchart sorts minerals by hardness, and stations may ask students to place specimens in order of increasing hardness.

cards.name: Streak
cards.cue: Colored, faintly colored, white, or whitish
cards.detail: The flowchart uses streak after hardness in several paths; competition examples note that two varieties of hematite can have different luster but the same streak.

cards.name: Cleavage and fracture
cards.cue: Rhombic cleavage, cubic cleavage, no cleavage, fracture
cards.detail: Stations may ask for a cleavage pattern, and practice property lists include rhombic cleavage, two directions of cleavage, and fracture.

cards.name: Density and luster clues
cards.detail: Practice property lists can ask students to match clues such as high density for a non-metallic mineral, low density for a metallic mineral, or fracture with submetallic appearance.

cards.name: Rock profile fields
cards.detail: Sedimentary rock tables organize evidence by particle size, composition, and physical properties before assigning a rock letter.

content.heading: First Field in the Mineral Flowchart
content.question: In the mineral identification flowchart, what is the first property to check?
choices: Particle size
Luster
Economic value
Rock letter
content.explanation: The mineral identification flowchart begins with luster, then branches to later checks such as hardness, streak, and cleavage.

misconception_by_choice.0: Particle size appears in a sedimentary rock table, not as the first step of the mineral flowchart.
misconception_by_choice.2: Economic value is discussed for ore minerals, but it is not the first flowchart decision.
misconception_by_choice.3: A rock letter is a table answer, not the first observed mineral property.

steps.label: Use only provided or allowed equipment
steps.detail: Stations may provide materials such as a copper cube, glass plate, and streak plate for testing hardness.

steps.label: Follow specimen cautions
steps.detail: A station may warn students not to test a particular point of a specimen.

steps.label: Do not scratch minerals against each other
steps.detail: The station direction specifically says not to scratch the minerals against each other.

steps.label: Record the property result, not just the action
steps.detail: Questions may ask students to identify specimens, record cleavage patterns, and order specimens by increasing hardness.

steps.label: Use diagnostic information when needed
steps.detail: When observable characteristics are not sufficient to identify a specimen, diagnostic properties may be provided.

content.heading: Allowed Testing
content.question: Which action conflicts with the station testing directions?
choices: Use the provided glass plate when testing is allowed.
Record the letter of each specimen in order of increasing hardness.
Scratch the minerals against each other to compare them directly.
Record the letter for a specimen’s cleavage pattern.
content.explanation: The station permits testing with provided materials, but it explicitly directs students not to scratch minerals against each other. A repeatable profile must follow the station’s testing limits.

misconception_by_choice.0: Using provided materials fits the station directions when testing is allowed.
misconception_by_choice.1: Ordering specimens by increasing hardness is one of the station tasks.
misconception_by_choice.3: Recording a cleavage-pattern letter is one of the station tasks.

content.heading: Worked Example: Turn Clues into a Profile
content.prompt: A practice station lists property clues such as high density for a non-metallic mineral, greasy and very soft, rhombic cleavage, two directions of cleavage with hardness of 6, and fracture with submetallic appearance. How do you record these without jumping straight to a name?
steps: Write the specimen or mineral label first, such as Mineral A, Mineral B, Mineral C, or Mineral D.
Treat each clue as evidence: density, surface appearance, softness or hardness, cleavage, and fracture/luster wording.
Keep the property clue separate from the final identification answer.
Use only the properties the task directs; a matching task may state that only four listed properties will be used.
After the evidence profile is organized, use it to make the identification or property match required by the station.

content.heading: Do Not Rely on One Appearance
content.question: A student sees two hematite samples with different luster and wants to identify them using luster alone. Which evidence habit best matches competition guidance?
choices: Use luster alone because two samples with different luster must be different minerals.
Record luster and streak, because hematite can show different luster while having the same streak.
Ignore streak because it is not used in mineral identification.
Skip observable characteristics and wait for the final answer.
content.explanation: The hematite example shows why one appearance feature can be incomplete: two varieties may differ in luster but share the same streak. Recording both properties creates a stronger evidence profile.

misconception_by_choice.0: Different luster alone is not enough here, because the example shows hematite varieties with different luster.
misconception_by_choice.2: Streak is used in the mineral identification flowchart and is highlighted in the hematite example.
misconception_by_choice.3: Observable characteristics are part of identification; when they are not sufficient, diagnostic properties may be provided.

content.heading: Key Points
points: Separate observations and test results from the final identification name.
A repeatable evidence profile uses organized physical-property fields such as luster, hardness, streak, cleavage, fracture, density, particle size, composition, and other station-provided clues.
Stations are timed, and there may be no return, so record useful evidence before moving on.
Follow testing directions exactly; use provided materials and do not scratch minerals against each other.
If observable characteristics are not enough, use diagnostic properties that are provided.
content.next_step: Practice with one unknown specimen: create a labeled evidence profile first, then write the identification as a separate conclusion.

units.title: Mineral Properties
units.summary: Use diagnostic physical properties instead of relying on color or first impressions.
objectives: Choose the next test that best separates remaining candidates.

skills.name: Color, Streak, and Luster
skills.description: Compare surface color, powdered streak, and luster and explain which observations are most diagnostic.

lesson.title: Color, Streak, and Luster
lesson.summary: Students compare surface color, powdered streak, and luster, then decide when each observation is useful or not useful for mineral identification.

content.kicker: Same color, different mineral. Different color, same mineral.
content.heading: Goal for Today
content.body: By the end of the lesson, you will compare surface color, powdered streak, and luster, then justify which observation is most diagnostic in at least three identification situations.

content.heading: Three Visual Clues: Color, Streak, and Luster
content.body: Mineral identification starts with what you can observe, but not every visual clue is equally dependable. Use these three clues together, then decide whether another property is needed.

cards.name: Surface color
cards.cue: What the outside of the specimen looks like
cards.detail: Color can vary within the same mineral species. Quartz occurs in many colors and forms, calcite may be colorless or white with other colors caused by impurities, and feldspar varieties range across several light and dark colors.

cards.name: Streak
cards.cue: The powdered mark made using a streak plate
cards.detail: A streak can be more diagnostic than outside color. Hematite is described with steel-gray color but a strong red-brown streak, while calcite may have many colors but has a white streak.

cards.name: Luster
cards.detail: Luster terms include vitreous, pearly, metallic, dull, earthy, resinous, greasy, silky, and satiny. Calcite is vitreous and may be pearly along cleavage surfaces; galena has bright metallic luster.

content.heading: Checkpoint 1: Color vs. Streak
content.question: A mineral is listed as having many possible surface colors but a white streak. Which observation is the better match to the mineral's powdered mark?
choices: Its outside color must be white every time.
Its streak is white even though the outside color can vary.
Its luster must be metallic.
Its hardness must be 7.
content.explanation: Calcite is described with many possible colors and a white streak. That means the powdered streak can stay white even when the surface color changes, so the streak gives a steadier clue than color alone.

misconception_by_choice.0: This treats surface color and streak as the same thing. The data show calcite can have many colors while keeping a white streak.
misconception_by_choice.2: Metallic luster is not supported here. Calcite is described as vitreous and may be pearly along cleavage surfaces.
misconception_by_choice.3: Hardness 7 describes quartz, not the mineral with many colors and white streak in this example.

content.heading: How to Decide Which Clue Is Most Diagnostic

steps.label: 1. Record luster first
steps.detail: Separate metallic from nonmetallic when the key does so. The flow chart uses metallic and nonmetallic branches, and it also lists luster types such as vitreous, pearly, and metallic.

steps.label: 2. Record color, but treat it cautiously
steps.detail: Color may vary. Quartz has varied colors, feldspar varieties vary in color, and calcite may be colorless or white with other colors from impurities.

steps.label: 3. Compare streak to surface color
steps.detail: A mismatch can be useful. Hematite is described as steel-gray in color but with a strong red-brown streak. Calcite may show many colors but has a white streak.

steps.label: 4. If the visual clues are not enough, switch to stronger properties
steps.detail: For colorless minerals, a tournament station identifies hardness and cleavage as the most useful properties, not color and streak.

content.heading: Checkpoint 2: Diagnostic Streak
content.question: A specimen has steel-gray color, no cleavage, hardness 5–6, and a strong red-brown streak. Which identification best fits?
choices: Graphite
Magnetite
Limonite
Hematite
content.explanation: The strongest match is hematite because it is listed with steel-gray color, no cleavage, hardness 5–6, and a strong red-brown streak. The streak is especially important because it is not the same as the outside color.

misconception_by_choice.0: Graphite is dark gray to black, very soft, greasy, and smudges fingers; that does not match hardness 5–6 with a strong red-brown streak.
misconception_by_choice.1: Magnetite is black, strongly magnetic, and has a black to gray streak; the red-brown streak does not fit.
misconception_by_choice.2: Limonite is described with yellow-brown to dark brown color and yellow, brown, or white streak, not a strong red-brown streak with steel-gray color.

content.heading: Worked Example: When Color and Luster Are Not Enough
content.prompt: Two specimens are light-colored and have vitreous luster. One may be calcite and one may be halite. How should you reason from color, streak, and luster?
steps: Start with color: both can be colorless or white, so color alone does not separate them.
Check luster: both are described with vitreous luster, so luster alone still does not separate them.
Use streak if it is available: calcite has a white streak, but that still may not separate it from other light-colored minerals.
Move to a more diagnostic property: calcite has three cleavages not at 90° and fizzes strongly with acid; halite commonly shows perfect cubic cleavage and tastes like salt.

content.heading: Checkpoint 3: Transfer to a Station
content.question: At a station with colorless minerals, which pair of properties is identified as most useful?
choices: Color and streak
Hardness and cleavage
Specific gravity and luster
Crystal habit and transparency
content.explanation: For colorless minerals, color does not give much separation. The station identifies hardness and cleavage as the most useful pair, so students should not rely on color and streak when those clues are weak.

misconception_by_choice.0: This is tempting because the lesson focuses on visual clues, but the station specifically treats colorless minerals as better identified by hardness and cleavage.
misconception_by_choice.2: Specific gravity and luster are listed as a choice, but they are not the selected most useful pair for the colorless minerals station.
misconception_by_choice.3: Crystal habit and transparency are also listed as a choice, but the station points to hardness and cleavage instead.

content.heading: Luster Helps, but It Usually Needs Partners
content.body: Luster is a strong first-sort clue, especially for separating metallic-looking specimens from nonmetallic-looking specimens. Still, several minerals can share the same luster, so pair luster with streak, color, hardness, cleavage, or special tests when needed.

cards.name: Vitreous
cards.detail: Feldspar has vitreous luster, quartz has vitreous to somewhat greasy luster, calcite is vitreous and may be pearly along cleavage surfaces, and several flow-chart minerals are listed with vitreous luster.

cards.name: Pearly, silky, satiny, greasy, dull, earthy, resinous
cards.detail: Calcite may be pearly along cleavage surfaces, gypsum may show silky or satiny luster in satin spar, graphite may feel greasy, sulfur may be resinous or vitreous, and limonite may be dull or earthy.

cards.name: Metallic
cards.detail: Galena is listed with bright metallic luster and lead-gray color. Pyrite has brass-yellow color and is called fool's gold. Graphite may have metallic luster but is very soft and smudges fingers.

content.heading: Checkpoint 4: Shared Luster
content.question: A specimen has vitreous luster and could be one of several colors. What is the safest identification move?
choices: Identify it as calcite immediately.
Use more evidence, because several minerals can have vitreous luster and many possible colors.
Decide it must be metallic.
Ignore streak because all vitreous minerals have the same streak.
content.explanation: Vitreous luster and variable color are not unique. Calcite, dolomite, and fluorite are all listed with vitreous luster and many possible colors in the flow chart, so more evidence is needed before identifying the specimen.

misconception_by_choice.0: Calcite can fit vitreous luster and variable color, but those clues are shared by other minerals, so they are not enough by themselves.
misconception_by_choice.2: Vitreous is a nonmetallic glassy luster, not metallic luster.
misconception_by_choice.3: Streak cannot be ignored. Minerals with similar luster can still differ in streak and other properties.

content.heading: Key Takeaways
points: Surface color is easy to observe, but it can vary within the same mineral.
Streak can be more diagnostic when the powdered color is steadier than the outside color, as with hematite's red-brown streak.
Luster is useful for sorting minerals, but shared luster terms like vitreous do not identify a specimen by themselves.
When color, streak, and luster are not enough, use stronger properties such as hardness, cleavage, acid reaction, magnetism, or other listed tests.
content.next_step: Practice with a small set of unknowns: record color, streak, and luster first, then write one sentence explaining whether those observations are enough to identify each mineral.

skills.name: Hardness and the Mohs Scale
skills.description: Bracket an unknown mineral's hardness with scratch tests and state the result without overclaiming.

lesson.title: Hardness and the Mohs Scale
lesson.summary: Students learn to use scratch tests with common hardness tools to bracket an unknown mineral's Mohs hardness and report the result as a range rather than an exact value.

content.kicker: Can one scratch tell the whole story?
content.heading: Goal: bracket hardness without overclaiming
content.body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to use scratch-test evidence from common hardness tools to state an unknown mineral's hardness as a supported bracket, such as harder than copper but not hard enough to scratch glass, instead of claiming an exact Mohs number without enough evidence.

content.heading: Mohs scale and common test tools
content.body: The Mohs scale orders minerals by hardness using whether one material can scratch another. Common tools help constrain, or bracket, the hardness of an unknown mineral.

cards.name: Mohs reference minerals
cards.detail: The scale lists talc at 1, gypsum at 2, calcite at 3, fluorite at 4, apatite at 5, orthoclase feldspar at 6, quartz at 7, topaz or beryl at 8, corundum at 9, and diamond at 10.

cards.name: Everyday hardness tools
cards.detail: A fingernail is about 2 to 2.5, a copper coin is about 3.5, glass is about 5 to 5.5, a steel knife or steel nail is about 5 to 6, and a streak plate is about 6.5 to 7.

cards.name: What hardness evidence means
cards.detail: A harder mineral can scratch a softer one. If two minerals have the same hardness, they may be able to scratch each other, so results should be stated carefully.

content.heading: Check the scale
content.question: Which common item gives the best evidence for testing whether an unknown mineral is harder than about 3.5?
choices: Copper coin
Fingernail
Streak plate
Diamond
content.explanation: A copper coin is listed at about 3.5, so if an unknown scratches copper, the unknown is harder than that test point. This gives a useful lower bracket.

misconception_by_choice.1: A fingernail is only about 2 to 2.5, so it tests a softer boundary than 3.5.
misconception_by_choice.2: A streak plate is much harder, about 6.5 to 7, so it does not test the 3.5 boundary.
misconception_by_choice.3: Diamond is the top Mohs reference mineral at 10, not a common bracket tool for the 3.5 level.

content.heading: How to make a valid scratch test

steps.label: Choose the surfaces
steps.detail: Use a sharp edge or point of a material with known hardness on a smooth face of the mineral being tested. Make sure the contact points are the materials you intend to test, not impurities.

steps.label: Make one controlled scratch
steps.detail: Do not rub back and forth like an eraser. Press hard and slowly scratch a line, like trying to etch a groove in glass.

steps.label: Check for a real groove
steps.detail: Sometimes powder from the softer material is left behind and can look like a scratch. Brush the tested surface with your finger and look for a groove or scratch that remains.

steps.label: Use magnification if needed
steps.detail: A hand lens or magnifying glass may be needed to decide whether a scratch was made.

steps.label: Double-check when appropriate
steps.detail: Results can be checked by trying the unknown mineral against the substance of known hardness. If two materials have the same hardness, they may be able to scratch each other.

content.heading: Scratch or powder?
content.question: During a test, a pale line appears on the surface. After brushing it with a finger, the line disappears. What is the best conclusion?
choices: It was probably powder, not a confirmed scratch.
The tested material was definitely scratched.
The unknown mineral must have hardness 7.
The two minerals must have exactly the same hardness.
content.explanation: A real scratch should remain as a groove or mark after loose powder is removed. A line that disappears after brushing fits the warning that powder from a softer material can imitate a scratch.

misconception_by_choice.1: A confirmed scratch requires evidence that a groove or scratch remains after brushing away powder.
misconception_by_choice.2: No evidence here connects the result to quartz or hardness 7.
misconception_by_choice.3: Equal hardness minerals may scratch each other, but a disappearing powder line does not show equal hardness.

content.heading: Using glass without overclaiming
content.body: Glass is a common hardness standard in mineral labs, but the test must be done in the correct direction and the result should be reported as a bracket.

cards.name: Why glass is useful
cards.detail: Glass is useful because scratches are easy to see on it, its hardness is about 5 to 5.5, and it is inexpensive and easily replaced.

cards.name: Correct glass test
cards.detail: Place the glass on a stable, flat surface and rub the mineral on the glass, then check whether the glass was scratched.

cards.name: Incorrect glass test
cards.cue: Do not use glass as the scratcher
cards.detail: Do not try to scratch the mineral with the glass because glass chips easily.

cards.name: What glass tells you
cards.cue: A bracket, not an exact number
cards.detail: If an unknown scratches glass, it is harder than the glass test point. If it does not scratch glass, the result only supports that it is not hard enough to scratch a material around 5 to 5.5.

content.heading: Choose the correct glass procedure
content.question: Which procedure matches the recommended glass hardness test?
choices: Put the glass on a stable, flat surface, rub the mineral on the glass, and check whether the glass was scratched.
Hold the mineral still and try to scratch it with the edge of the glass.
Rub the mineral back and forth on the glass like an eraser until powder appears.
Scratch two unknown minerals against each other and ignore the glass.
content.explanation: The recommended procedure is to place the glass on a stable, flat surface and rub the mineral on the glass. Glass should not be used to scratch the mineral because it chips easily, and rubbing back and forth can confuse powder with a true scratch.

misconception_by_choice.1: Glass should not be used to scratch the mineral because it chips easily.
misconception_by_choice.2: The scratch should be a slow line, not back-and-forth rubbing like an eraser.
misconception_by_choice.3: Hardness stations provide tools such as copper, glass, and streak plate; scratching minerals against each other may be disallowed in station directions.

content.heading: Bracket an unknown from two tests
content.prompt: An unknown mineral scratches a copper penny but does not scratch glass. State the hardness evidence without overclaiming.
steps: Copper coin is about 3.5, so scratching copper supports that the unknown is harder than 3.5.
Glass is about 5 to 5.5, so not scratching glass supports that the unknown is not hard enough to scratch a material in that range.
A careful statement is: the unknown is harder than copper, about greater than 3.5, but below the glass test range of about 5 to 5.5.
Do not claim a single exact hardness number from only these two tests.

content.heading: Report the bracket
content.question: A sample scratches copper but not glass. Which statement best reports the hardness evidence?
choices: Its hardness is bracketed above 3.5 and below the glass range of about 5 to 5.5.
Its hardness is exactly 4.0.
Its hardness is exactly 5.5 because glass is 5.5.
It must be diamond because it scratched a metal.
content.explanation: Copper gives a lower test point of about 3.5, and glass gives an upper test point of about 5 to 5.5 when the sample cannot scratch it. The evidence brackets hardness but does not justify a single exact value.

misconception_by_choice.1: The tests do not identify an exact Mohs number; they only place the sample between test limits.
misconception_by_choice.2: Not scratching glass does not mean the sample equals glass hardness.
misconception_by_choice.3: Diamond is Mohs 10, and scratching copper alone is not evidence for that extreme hardness.

content.heading: Turn scratch results into a competition answer

steps.label: List each test result
steps.detail: Record whether the unknown scratches each provided tool, such as copper, glass, or a streak plate.

steps.label: Convert tools to hardness bounds
steps.detail: Use the tool hardnesses: copper coin about 3.5, glass about 5 to 5.5, steel knife or nail about 5 to 6, and streak plate about 6.5 to 7.

steps.label: Keep the result as a range
steps.detail: State the bracket supported by the tests instead of turning the result into an exact Mohs number.

steps.label: Use hardness with other properties
steps.detail: Hardness is often combined with other properties such as cleavage when identifying minerals, especially in station work.

content.heading: Avoid the wrong meaning of Mohs hardness
content.question: Which statement is NOT true of the Mohs scale of hardness?
choices: It measures hardness by how easily a mineral resists breaking.
It compares hardness by seeing which minerals can scratch others.
It was created by Friedrich Mohs.
Diamond is the hardest mineral listed on the scale.
content.explanation: Mohs hardness is based on scratching relationships, not on resistance to breaking. The scale is associated with Friedrich Mohs, and diamond is listed at 10 at the top of the scale.

misconception_by_choice.1: This is a true description of the scratch-comparison basis of Mohs hardness.
misconception_by_choice.2: This is true; the scale is named for Friedrich Mohs.
misconception_by_choice.3: This is true for the listed Mohs scale, where diamond is 10.

content.heading: Key points for bracketing hardness
points: Mohs hardness uses scratch comparisons: harder materials scratch softer materials.
Common tools give useful bounds: fingernail 2 to 2.5, copper coin about 3.5, glass about 5 to 5.5, steel knife or nail about 5 to 6, and streak plate about 6.5 to 7.
A valid scratch test needs a slow single line, correct contact points, and a check that a real groove remains after powder is brushed away.
Glass is tested by rubbing the mineral on glass, not by scratching the mineral with glass.
Report what the evidence supports: a bracketed range, not an exact hardness unless the evidence justifies it.
content.next_step: Practice with an unknown sample: test it against copper, glass, and a streak plate, then write one sentence that states only the supported hardness bracket.

skills.name: Breakage, Density, and Special Properties
skills.description: Use cleavage, fracture, density, magnetism, and acid reaction to narrow an identification.

lesson.title: Breakage, Density, and Special Properties
lesson.summary: Students learn how cleavage, fracture, density or specific gravity clues, magnetism, and acid reaction can narrow mineral identification choices.

content.heading: Goal: Narrow an identification using five evidence types
content.body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to use breakage pattern, density or specific gravity clues, magnetism, and acid reaction to eliminate choices and choose a better mineral identification.

content.heading: Breakage: cleavage directions versus fracture
content.body: Breakage is useful because some minerals split along flat cleavage planes, while others show fracture surfaces instead. The key is to count directions, not the number of visible faces.

cards.name: Count nonparallel cleavage surfaces
cards.cue: Ask: Which flat surfaces are not parallel to each other?
cards.detail: A specimen can show several visible cleavage surfaces, but parallel surfaces count as one cleavage direction.

cards.name: One cleavage direction
cards.cue: Repeated flat sheets or surfaces all parallel
cards.detail: Minerals with one cleavage are often described as having basal cleavage.

cards.name: Two cleavage directions
cards.detail: Two directions may meet at 90 degrees, or they may meet at angles such as 56 degrees and 124 degrees.

cards.name: Three cleavage directions
cards.detail: Halite has three directions at 90 degrees. Calcite is listed with three directions not at 90 degrees, and calcite cleavage is described as rhombic.

cards.name: Fracture
cards.detail: Some specimens are described by fracture terms, such as conchoidal to uneven fracture, rather than by cleavage directions.

content.heading: Checkpoint: Count cleavage directions
content.question: A mineral shows a flat surface on top, another flat surface on the bottom, and a third flat surface lying on the table. All three surfaces are parallel to each other. How many cleavage directions should you record?
choices: One cleavage direction
Two cleavage directions
Three cleavage directions
No cleavage
content.explanation: Cleavage directions are counted by finding cleavage surfaces that are not parallel to each other. If all visible flat cleavage surfaces are parallel, they count as one direction, even if several faces are visible.

misconception_by_choice.1: This counts the number of visible faces instead of checking whether the surfaces are nonparallel.
misconception_by_choice.2: This treats each visible surface as a separate direction, but parallel cleavage faces do not add new directions.
misconception_by_choice.3: This ignores the flat, repeated cleavage surfaces. No cleavage would fit a specimen described by fracture instead.

content.heading: Acid reaction: use speed and strength of bubbling

steps.label: Use a small drop
steps.detail: Only a small drop of dilute hydrochloric acid is needed to see whether a mineral bubbles.

steps.label: Watch for calcite
steps.detail: Calcite reacts readily with dilute hydrochloric acid by bubbling or effervescing and releasing carbon dioxide. It is also described as fizzing strongly with the acid test.

steps.label: Compare dolomite carefully
steps.detail: Dolomite reacts much more slowly unless it is powdered first; weak acid may show little or no visible bubbling.

steps.label: Use safe cleanup
steps.detail: Dilute acid can burn skin or damage clothing, so the acid should be washed off the mineral immediately after the test, and skin or clothing should be rinsed right away if acid gets on them.

content.heading: Checkpoint: Acid test evidence
content.question: Two carbonate minerals are tested with a small drop of dilute hydrochloric acid. Sample A bubbles readily. Sample B reacts much more slowly unless powdered. Which identification is best supported?
choices: Sample A is calcite; Sample B is dolomite
Sample A is dolomite; Sample B is calcite
Both samples must be magnetite
Both samples must be halite
content.explanation: Calcite readily effervesces with dilute hydrochloric acid. Dolomite is also a carbonate mineral, but its reaction is much slower unless the mineral is powdered first.

misconception_by_choice.1: This reverses the key acid evidence: the fast, ready bubbling fits calcite, while the slower powdered reaction fits dolomite.
misconception_by_choice.2: Magnetite is identified by strong magnetism, not by the carbonate acid reaction described here.
misconception_by_choice.3: Halite is listed with cubic cleavage and a salty taste, not as the mineral that distinguishes itself by this acid reaction pattern.

content.heading: Special properties and density clues
content.body: Some properties are especially useful because they can quickly reduce the number of possible minerals. Magnetism, specific gravity, and high density descriptions should be combined with breakage and luster evidence.

cards.name: Magnetism
cards.cue: Bring the hand magnet and mineral together
cards.detail: Magnetite is the only common mineral described as strongly magnetic. It is also listed as black, hardness 5.5 to 6, and with no cleavage.

cards.name: Galena density clue
cards.cue: Very heavy metallic sample with cubic cleavage
cards.detail: Galena has metallic luster, three perfect cleavages that intersect at 90 degrees, and very high specific gravity listed as 7.5.

cards.name: Specific gravity as station evidence
cards.cue: Use the number as another clue, not as a guess
cards.detail: Identification stations may give specific gravity values, such as 2.06, 8.96, 10.5, and 19.3, or ask students to match a property such as high density for a non-metallic mineral.

cards.name: Do not stop at one clue
cards.detail: A strong identification uses multiple properties, such as magnetism plus no cleavage for magnetite, or very high specific gravity plus three cleavages at 90 degrees for galena.

content.heading: Checkpoint: Magnetism as a narrowing clue
content.question: An unknown mineral is black, has hardness 5.5 to 6, shows no cleavage, and is strongly attracted to a hand magnet. Which identification is best supported?
choices: Magnetite
Galena
Calcite
Halite
content.explanation: The strongest evidence is magnetism: magnetite is described as the only common mineral likely to be strongly magnetic. The additional clues of black color, hardness 5.5 to 6, and no cleavage also match the listed magnetite properties.

misconception_by_choice.1: Galena is described by metallic luster, very high specific gravity, and three perfect cleavages at 90 degrees, not strong magnetism with no cleavage.
misconception_by_choice.2: Calcite is identified by rhombic cleavage and strong acid reaction, not by strong attraction to a magnet.
misconception_by_choice.3: Halite is listed with perfect cubic cleavage and salty taste, not as strongly magnetic.

content.heading: Worked example: Narrow a mineral using breakage and acid
content.prompt: Unknown X is nonmetallic, softer than glass, has three cleavage directions not at 90 degrees, and reacts strongly with acid. What identification is best supported?
steps: Start with the nonmetallic, softer-than-glass branch because those are broad sorting clues.
Use breakage next: three cleavage directions not at 90 degrees points toward the rhombic-cleavage carbonate choice.
Use the acid reaction to separate the choices: strong fizzing fits calcite.
Final identification: calcite, because calcite has three rhombic cleavage directions and fizzes strongly with acid.

content.heading: Checkpoint: Transfer to a dense metallic mineral
content.question: A metallic mineral has three perfect cleavage directions intersecting at 90 degrees and a very high specific gravity of 7.5. Which mineral is best supported by those combined clues?
choices: Calcite
Magnetite
Galena
Dolomite
content.explanation: Galena is described with obvious metallic luster, three perfect cleavages intersecting at 90 degrees, and very high specific gravity of 7.5. The identification is stronger because all three clues point to the same mineral.

misconception_by_choice.0: Calcite has rhombic cleavage and strong acid reaction, not metallic luster with very high specific gravity of 7.5.
misconception_by_choice.1: Magnetite is strongly magnetic and has no cleavage, so three perfect cleavages at 90 degrees do not fit.
misconception_by_choice.3: Dolomite is separated from calcite by its slower acid reaction unless powdered; the metallic luster, cubic cleavage pattern, and specific gravity clue fit galena instead.

content.heading: Key points for identification
points: Count cleavage directions by counting nonparallel cleavage surfaces, not every visible face.
Fracture is used when breakage is irregular or described by fracture terms rather than cleavage directions.
Calcite fizzes strongly with acid; dolomite reacts much more slowly unless powdered.
Magnetite is the common strongly magnetic mineral and is listed with no cleavage.
Specific gravity and density clues are strongest when combined with other evidence, such as galena’s metallic luster and three cleavages at 90 degrees.
content.next_step: Practice with an evidence table: list breakage, density or specific gravity, magnetism, and acid reaction before choosing a final mineral name.

units.title: The Rock Cycle
units.summary: Explain rock change as a set of processes rather than a single circular path.
objectives: Interpret more than one valid path through the rock cycle.

skills.name: Processes That Change Rock
skills.description: Connect melting, cooling, weathering, erosion, deposition, lithification, heat, and pressure to rock change.

lesson.title: Processes That Change Rock
lesson.summary: Students connect rock-cycle processes to changes among igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks, focusing on melting, solidification, weathering, erosion, deposition, cementation and compaction, heat, and pressure.

content.kicker: A rock can change without staying in the same group.
content.heading: Goal for Today
content.body: By the end of this lesson, given a before-and-after rock scenario, you will choose the process and the resulting rock group correctly in at least 3 out of 4 checkpoints.

content.heading: The Three Rock Groups Are Named by How They Form
content.body: Use formation process first. Do not start by guessing color, size, or a single mineral.

cards.name: Igneous
cards.detail: Igneous rocks form from the solidification of molten magma or lava. They may form below the surface as magma solidifies or at the surface during a volcanic eruption.

cards.name: Sedimentary
cards.cue: Weathered sediments are cemented and compacted
cards.detail: Sedimentary rocks form from the cementation and compaction of weathered materials called sediments.

cards.name: Metamorphic
cards.cue: Existing rock experiences intense heat and pressure
cards.detail: Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are subjected to intense heat and pressure.

content.heading: Check: Formation Clue
content.question: A rock forms when molten lava solidifies at Earth’s surface during a volcanic eruption. Which rock group fits that evidence?
choices: Igneous
Sedimentary
Metamorphic
Mineral
content.explanation: Igneous rocks form from the solidification of molten magma or lava, including at the surface during a volcanic eruption. The key evidence is molten material becoming solid.

misconception_by_choice.1: Sedimentary rocks form from weathered sediments that are cemented and compacted, not from molten lava.
misconception_by_choice.2: Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks experience intense heat and pressure, not when lava solidifies.
misconception_by_choice.3: A mineral is not one of the three rock groups classified by rock formation process.

content.heading: Decision Steps for a Rock-Change Scenario

steps.label: Step 1: Look for molten material
steps.detail: If magma or lava is involved and then solidifies, the result is igneous rock.

steps.label: Step 2: Look for intense heat and pressure
steps.detail: If an existing rock is changed by intense heat and pressure, the result is metamorphic rock.

steps.label: Step 3: Look for weathered materials called sediments
steps.detail: If weathered sediments are cemented and compacted, the result is sedimentary rock.

steps.label: Step 4: Track the starting rock separately
steps.detail: Rock-cycle questions may start with sedimentary, metamorphic, or igneous rocks and ask what must happen next, such as forming magma or becoming exposed to weathering and erosion.

content.heading: Check: Heat and Pressure
content.question: An existing igneous rock is acted on by heat and pressure. Which change is best supported?
choices: It becomes a mineral because all rocks have exact compositions.
It becomes metamorphic rock.
It becomes sedimentary rock because it was once solid.
It becomes igneous rock because heat is involved.
content.explanation: Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are subjected to intense heat and pressure. The worksheet also connects heat and pressure acting on igneous rocks with a rock-change result.

misconception_by_choice.0: Rocks do not have definite chemical compositions, and this scenario is asking for a rock group formed by a process.
misconception_by_choice.2: Sedimentary rocks form from cementation and compaction of weathered sediments; that process is not described here.
misconception_by_choice.3: Igneous rocks form from solidification of molten magma or lava. Heat alone is not the formation clue for igneous rock.

content.heading: Process Vocabulary: What Each Word Signals
content.body: In Science Olympiad questions, process words are evidence. Match the word to the kind of change it describes.

cards.name: Melting
cards.detail: Magma and lava are molten materials. A worksheet prompt asks what must happen to sedimentary, metamorphic, or igneous rocks in order to form magma.

cards.name: Solidification
cards.cue: Molten magma or lava becomes rock
cards.detail: Solidification of molten magma or lava forms igneous rock.

cards.name: Weathering and erosion
cards.cue: Exposed rocks are connected to surface processes
cards.detail: The worksheet pairs weathering and erosion with exposed rocks. Weathered materials are called sediments.

cards.name: Cementation and compaction
cards.detail: Sedimentary rocks form from cementation and compaction of weathered materials called sediments.

cards.name: Recrystallization of un-melted material
cards.detail: The worksheet connects recrystallization of un-melted material with a rock type, and the formation description for metamorphic rocks is intense heat and pressure acting on existing rocks.

content.heading: Check: Sedimentary Path
content.question: Which process set best explains how weathered materials become a sedimentary rock?
choices: Melting, then solidification
Intense heat and pressure
Cementation and compaction of sediments
Recrystallization of un-melted material
content.explanation: Sedimentary rocks form from weathered materials called sediments when those sediments are cemented and compacted. The process set must include sediments, cementation, and compaction.

misconception_by_choice.0: Melting followed by solidification points to igneous rock, not sedimentary rock.
misconception_by_choice.1: Intense heat and pressure point to metamorphic rock, not sedimentary rock.
misconception_by_choice.3: Recrystallization of un-melted material connects to metamorphic change, not sedimentary formation from sediments.

content.heading: Worked Example: Granite to Sandstone to Quartzite
content.prompt: A worksheet asks for the events needed for sandstone to form from granite, and then asks how that sandstone would become quartzite.
steps: Start by naming the starting material: granite is a rock example.
To make sandstone from granite, use the sedimentary pathway: weathered materials become sediments, and sedimentary rock forms when sediments are cemented and compacted.
To change sandstone into quartzite, use the metamorphic pathway: an existing rock is subjected to intense heat and pressure.

Do not use melting for the sandstone-to-quartzite step, because metamorphic formation is tied to heat and pressure on existing rock, while igneous formation is tied to solidification of molten material.

content.heading: Check: Transfer a Pathway
content.question: A team needs to explain how sandstone could become quartzite. Which answer best matches the rock-cycle evidence?
choices: The sandstone melts into magma and then solidifies.
The sandstone is cemented and compacted again.
The sandstone is subjected to intense heat and pressure.
The sandstone becomes a mineral with a definite chemical composition.
content.explanation: Quartzite is presented as the result of changing sandstone in the worksheet prompt. The supported process for changing an existing rock into a metamorphic rock is intense heat and pressure.

misconception_by_choice.0: Melting followed by solidification is the igneous pathway, not the metamorphic pathway used for sandstone to quartzite.
misconception_by_choice.1: Cementation and compaction form sedimentary rock from sediments; sandstone is already the rock being changed in this scenario.
misconception_by_choice.3: Rocks are mixtures and do not have definite chemical compositions like minerals.

content.heading: Answering Rock-Cycle Questions Under Time Pressure

steps.label: Underline the starting material
steps.detail: Examples might name an igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic rock, or may use a rock example such as granite or sandstone.

steps.label: Circle the process clue
steps.detail: Look for solidification, molten material, weathered sediments, cementation and compaction, heat and pressure, or recrystallization of un-melted material.

steps.label: Name the resulting group
steps.detail: Solidification of molten material points to igneous; cementation and compaction of sediments point to sedimentary; intense heat and pressure point to metamorphic.

steps.label: Keep identification and process separate
steps.detail: Science Olympiad Rocks and Minerals requires students to identify and classify rocks and minerals and also use that knowledge to explain geological processes.

content.heading: Check: Full Cycle Link
content.question: Which chain correctly connects an existing rock to magma and then to an igneous rock?
choices: Heat and pressure, then cementation and compaction
Weathering, then recrystallization of un-melted material
Melting to molten material, then solidification
Deposition, then exposure to weathering and erosion
content.explanation: Magma and lava are molten materials, and igneous rocks form when molten magma or lava solidifies. So the chain must include becoming molten and then solidifying.

misconception_by_choice.0: Heat and pressure point to metamorphic change, while cementation and compaction point to sedimentary formation.
misconception_by_choice.1: Weathering connects to sediments, and recrystallization of un-melted material does not describe forming magma.
misconception_by_choice.3: Deposition and exposure to weathering and erosion do not describe molten material solidifying into igneous rock.

content.heading: Key Points
points: Rocks are classified based on how they form: igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic.
Igneous rock forms when molten magma or lava solidifies.
Sedimentary rock forms when weathered materials called sediments are cemented and compacted.
Metamorphic rock forms when existing rock is subjected to intense heat and pressure.
For rock-cycle scenarios, track the starting rock, the process clue, and the resulting rock group.
content.next_step: Practice with three new before-and-after scenarios and write the process chain for each one before choosing the rock group.

skills.name: Reason Through Rock-Cycle Paths
skills.description: Trace and defend multiple possible transformations between rock types.

lesson.title: Reason Through Rock-Cycle Paths
lesson.summary: Students use formation evidence to trace and defend more than one possible transformation among igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks.

content.heading: Goal for Today
content.body: By the end of the lesson, you will trace and defend at least two possible transformations between rock types by naming the starting material, the process, and the rock type that forms.

content.heading: Three Formation Anchors
content.body: Use these anchors whenever you defend a rock-cycle path. The strongest answer names both the material being changed and the process that changes it.

cards.name: Igneous rock
cards.detail: Igneous rocks form from the solidification of molten magma or lava. Magma cooling is connected to forming igneous rock.

cards.name: Sedimentary rock
cards.detail: Sedimentary rocks form from the cementation and compaction of weathered materials called sediments.

cards.name: Metamorphic rock
cards.cue: Existing rock gets intense heat and pressure
cards.detail: Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are subjected to intense heat and pressure.

content.heading: Formation Anchor Check
content.question: Which choice correctly matches a rock type with the evidence for how it forms?
choices: Igneous rock forms when sediments are compacted and cemented.
Sedimentary rock forms from solidification of molten magma or lava.
Metamorphic rock forms when existing rocks are subjected to intense heat and pressure.
Sedimentary rock forms when magma cools underground.
content.explanation: Metamorphic rock is defined by a change to an already existing rock under intense heat and pressure. That makes choice 2 the only match that uses the correct starting material and process.

misconception_by_choice.0: This swaps the sedimentary process onto igneous rock. Compaction and cementation of sediments form sedimentary rock.
misconception_by_choice.1: This assigns the igneous process to sedimentary rock. Solidification of molten magma or lava forms igneous rock.
misconception_by_choice.3: Cooling magma is tied to igneous rock, not sedimentary rock.

content.heading: How to Defend a Rock-Cycle Path

steps.label: 1. Name the starting material
steps.detail: Start with the evidence you are given, such as magma, sediments, or an existing rock.

steps.label: 2. Choose the process that fits that material
steps.detail: Molten magma or lava solidifies to form igneous rock; sediments become sedimentary rock by compaction and cementation; existing rock becomes metamorphic rock under intense heat and pressure.

steps.label: 3. Name the rock type produced
steps.detail: The process determines whether the result is igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic.

steps.label: 4. Chain steps when needed
steps.detail: If the starting material is not the direct input for the final rock type, build a multi-step path using the formation anchors.

content.heading: Apply the Path Rule
content.question: A team traces this path: sediments → sedimentary rock → metamorphic rock. Which defense best fits the evidence?
choices: Sediments first become sedimentary rock by compaction and cementation, then that existing rock can become metamorphic under intense heat and pressure.
Sediments first melt into magma, then pressure alone makes metamorphic rock.
Sediments become igneous rock by cementation, then igneous rock is automatically metamorphic.
Sediments become metamorphic rock by cooling, then the rock becomes sedimentary by heat and pressure.
content.explanation: The first step uses the sedimentary process: compaction and cementation of sediments. The second step uses the metamorphic process: intense heat and pressure acting on an existing rock. That makes the path defensible.

misconception_by_choice.1: This adds melting and pressure alone, but the evidence given for metamorphic formation is intense heat and pressure acting on existing rock.
misconception_by_choice.2: Cementation and compaction of sediments form sedimentary rock, not igneous rock. Also, a rock does not become metamorphic automatically; the process is intense heat and pressure.
misconception_by_choice.3: Cooling is tied to igneous formation from molten material, not metamorphic formation. Heat and pressure form metamorphic rock, not sedimentary rock.

content.heading: Worked Example: From Magma to Metamorphic Rock
content.prompt: Trace and defend one possible path from magma to metamorphic rock.
steps: Start with magma. As molten magma or lava solidifies, it forms igneous rock.
Now the igneous rock is an existing rock.
If that existing rock is subjected to intense heat and pressure, it can form metamorphic rock.
Defensible path: magma → igneous rock → metamorphic rock, with solidification first and intense heat plus pressure second.

content.heading: Transfer to a New Route
content.question: Which sequence best supports a possible path from magma to sedimentary rock?
choices: Magma is compacted and cemented directly into sedimentary rock.
Magma solidifies into igneous rock; weathered materials called sediments are then compacted and cemented into sedimentary rock.
Magma becomes metamorphic rock by cooling; metamorphic rock then becomes sedimentary rock by solidification.
Magma becomes sedimentary rock by intense heat and pressure.
content.explanation: The sequence uses the correct formation evidence in order: solidification of molten material forms igneous rock, and sedimentary rock forms from sediments by compaction and cementation.

misconception_by_choice.0: Compaction and cementation act on sediments, not directly on magma.
misconception_by_choice.2: Cooling or solidification of molten material forms igneous rock, not metamorphic rock. Solidification is also not the sedimentary process.
misconception_by_choice.3: Intense heat and pressure acting on existing rock form metamorphic rock, not sedimentary rock.

content.heading: Sedimentary Endpoints: Match Sediment to Rock
content.body: When a path ends in sedimentary rock, sediment evidence can help defend which sedimentary rock could form.

cards.name: Beach or sand dunes
cards.detail: Sand in a beach or sand-dune environment can form sandstone.

cards.name: Deep lake, tidal flat, lagoon, or river floodplain
cards.detail: Mud in these environments can form shale.

cards.name: River bed
cards.detail: Rounded pebbles and cobbles in a river bed can form conglomerate.

cards.name: Alluvial fan or glacier area
cards.detail: Unrounded pebbles and cobbles in these environments can form breccia.

cards.name: Coral reef
cards.detail: Carbonate sand in a coral reef can form limestone.

cards.name: River delta
cards.detail: Sand and mud in a river delta can form sandstone and shale.

content.heading: Use Sediment Evidence
content.question: A team says a sedimentary rock formed from carbonate sand in a coral reef environment. Which rock best fits that evidence?
choices: Breccia
Limestone
Shale
Rock salt
content.explanation: Carbonate sand in a coral reef environment is matched with limestone. The correct answer uses both the sediment clue and the environment clue.

misconception_by_choice.0: Breccia is matched with unrounded pebbles and cobbles in environments such as an alluvial fan or glacier area, not carbonate sand in a coral reef.
misconception_by_choice.2: Shale is matched with mud in several environments, not carbonate sand in a coral reef.
misconception_by_choice.3: Rock salt is matched with a desert lake setting, not carbonate sand in a coral reef.

content.heading: Key Points
points: Rock-cycle reasoning depends on formation evidence: starting material plus process.
Igneous rock forms when molten magma or lava solidifies.
Sedimentary rock forms when sediments are compacted and cemented.
Metamorphic rock forms when existing rock is changed by intense heat and pressure.
A defensible path may need more than one step, as long as each step uses the correct process.
Sediment evidence, such as sand, mud, rounded pebbles, unrounded pebbles, or carbonate sand, can help defend a sedimentary endpoint.
content.next_step: Practice by drawing two different rock-cycle paths and writing one sentence of evidence for each arrow.

units.title: Igneous Rocks
units.summary: Read cooling history from texture and connect mineral composition to classification.
objectives: Classify common igneous specimens with texture and composition together.

skills.name: Cooling History and Igneous Texture
skills.description: Infer intrusive or extrusive cooling history from crystal size and texture.

lesson.title: Cooling History and Igneous Texture
lesson.summary: Students learn to use crystal size and texture evidence to infer intrusive or extrusive igneous history, with emphasis on coarse intergrown crystals, holes from gases, and tournament-style texture categories.

content.heading: Goal: Infer cooling history from texture evidence
content.body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to choose whether an igneous rock is intrusive or extrusive when given crystal-size and texture clues, especially coarse intergrown crystals and holes from gases.

content.heading: Core texture clues for intrusive and extrusive igneous rocks
content.body: In tournament questions, the best clue is often the texture, not the rock’s color or composition word.

cards.name: Coarse-grained intergrown crystals
cards.cue: Crystals are coarse and grown together.
cards.detail: This was the keyed characteristic used to classify Specimen A as an intrusive igneous rock.

cards.name: Holes from gases
cards.cue: The rock has holes left by gases.
cards.detail: This was the keyed characteristic used to classify Specimen B as an extrusive igneous rock.

cards.name: Composition words are separate evidence
cards.cue: Felsic, intermediate, and mafic describe composition.
cards.detail: The classification table separates composition from texture, so composition should not replace texture evidence when the question asks for intrusive or extrusive clues.

content.heading: Check the intrusive clue
content.question: Which characteristic best supports classifying Specimen A as an intrusive igneous rock?
choices: Felsic composition
Coarse-grained intergrown crystals
Mafic composition
Fine-grained intergrown crystals
content.explanation: Coarse-grained intergrown crystals are the keyed evidence for Specimen A being intrusive. The key separates this texture clue from composition choices such as felsic or mafic.

misconception_by_choice.0: Felsic is a composition term, but the keyed intrusive clue for Specimen A is texture.
misconception_by_choice.2: Mafic is also a composition term, not the keyed intrusive evidence for Specimen A.
misconception_by_choice.3: Fine-grained intergrown crystals were not the keyed characteristic for classifying Specimen A as intrusive.

content.heading: A decision routine for cooling-history questions

steps.label: 1. Identify what the question asks
steps.detail: If the question asks intrusive or extrusive, look for texture clues before using composition words.

steps.label: 2. Look for coarse intergrown crystals
steps.detail: Coarse-grained intergrown crystals are the keyed clue for intrusive classification.

steps.label: 3. Look for holes from gases
steps.detail: Holes from gases are the keyed clue for extrusive classification.

steps.label: 4. Keep texture and composition separate
steps.detail: Tournament tables may ask for both texture and composition, using texture rows such as glassy, vesicular, aphanitic, and phaneritic and composition columns such as felsic, intermediate, and mafic.

content.heading: Apply the extrusive clue
content.question: A rock sample is described as having holes from gases. Based on the keyed evidence, which classification is best supported?
choices: Extrusive igneous rock
Intrusive igneous rock
Felsic igneous rock
Intermediate igneous rock
content.explanation: Holes from gases are the keyed characteristic used to classify Specimen B as extrusive. Felsic and intermediate are composition labels, while the evidence here is a texture feature.

misconception_by_choice.1: Intrusive classification was supported by coarse-grained intergrown crystals, not by holes from gases.
misconception_by_choice.2: Felsic is a composition category and does not match the keyed extrusive clue in this item.
misconception_by_choice.3: Intermediate is also a composition category, not the texture clue used for extrusive classification.

content.heading: Worked example: reading the evidence before choosing
content.prompt: A station asks which characteristic helps classify Specimen A as intrusive and which characteristic helps classify Specimen B as extrusive.
steps: For Specimen A, compare the options. The keyed choice is coarse-grained intergrown crystals.
Connect that clue to the classification: coarse-grained intergrown crystals support intrusive igneous classification.
For Specimen B, compare the options. The keyed choice is holes from gases.
Connect that clue to the classification: holes from gases support extrusive igneous classification.
Do not choose composition words, color, or density when the keyed evidence is texture.

content.heading: Avoid distractors
content.question: Which answer best explains why “mafic composition” was not the best evidence for classifying Specimen B as extrusive?
choices: Mafic composition means the rock must be intrusive.
Mafic composition is a composition clue, while the keyed extrusive evidence was holes from gases.
Mafic composition means the rock must be glassy.
Mafic composition means the rock has no texture.
content.explanation: The keyed evidence for Specimen B being extrusive was holes from gases. Mafic belongs to the composition side of classification, so it does not replace the texture clue.

misconception_by_choice.0: The evidence does not state that mafic composition automatically means intrusive.
misconception_by_choice.2: The evidence does not state that mafic composition automatically means glassy.
misconception_by_choice.3: The classification table uses both composition and texture, so mafic composition does not mean texture is absent.

content.heading: Texture categories used in igneous classification tables
content.body: Some questions ask you to place rocks in a table by both composition and texture. Keep the row label and column label separate.

cards.name: Glassy
cards.detail: Specimen D is placed in the felsic-glassy cell.

cards.name: Vesicular
cards.detail: Specimen B is placed in the mafic-vesicular cell, and holes from gases were the keyed extrusive clue for Specimen B.

cards.name: Aphanitic
cards.detail: Specimen C is placed in the felsic-aphanitic cell and is identified as rhyolite.

cards.name: Phaneritic
cards.detail: Specimens F, A, and E are placed in phaneritic cells across felsic, intermediate, and mafic compositions.

content.heading: Transfer to a table clue
content.question: Specimen A is placed in the intermediate-phaneritic cell, and the same station keys Specimen A’s intrusive clue as coarse-grained intergrown crystals. What should you infer from this evidence?
choices: For this specimen, phaneritic texture is being used with coarse intergrown crystals to support intrusive classification.
Intermediate composition alone proves the rock is extrusive.
Phaneritic texture means the specimen must be vesicular.
